opus-5.5.text:
I think it's mostly something you develop through experience, and honestly through a lot of failure. Early on, most of us can't really tell an important problem from one that's just technically interesting. You pick something because it looks hard or elegant, spend months on it, and then realize nobody actually needs the answer.

A few things helped me. First, being close to real users. When I worked on computer graphics and simulation, I kept running into the same frustration: writing high-performance physics code was painful. Researchers spent most of their time fighting low-level details instead of thinking about the actual physics. When you feel a pain point yourself, and you see many other people feeling it too, that's usually a strong signal the problem matters.

Second, I ask myself: if this works, what changes? If the answer is "I get a slightly better number on a benchmark," that's probably not very important. If it's "a whole group of people can now do something they couldn't do before," that's worth investing in.

Third, good mentors and good taste around you. You absorb a lot just by watching how experienced researchers choose and drop problems. They're often willing to abandon things quickly, and that's a skill too.

And finally, I think you have to just try. You make a bet, you see how the community reacts, whether people actually use what you built, and you calibrate. Over time, your intuition gets sharper. It's never perfect, but it gets better.

r001.rationale: The response mentions learning through failure and watching how the community reacts, but does not identify reflecting on disappointing reception of one’s own papers as a way to recognize important problems.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because honestly I don't think it's something you can learn from a textbook. It mostly comes from taste, and taste comes from exposure.

When I was a PhD student at MIT, the thing that shaped me most wasn't any single paper, it was being around people who had already made important things and watching how they talked about problems. You start to notice that they don't ask "is this publishable," they ask "if this worked, who would care, and for how long." That's a very different filter. A lot of problems are interesting for a week. Very few are interesting for ten years.

The second thing is that you have to actually build. With Taichi, I didn't set out thinking "I am going to work on an important problem." I was frustrated. I wanted to write physics simulations and the existing tools made it painful, and I wrote code to make my own life easier. Only later did I realize that a lot of other people had the same pain, and that the pain was pointing at something real. So I would say pain is a really good signal. If something keeps annoying you and everyone just accepts it, that is often where an important problem is hiding.

The third part is being honest with yourself about whether something is important or just hard. Those get confused all the time, especially in academia, because hard things look impressive. But hard and important are orthogonal. Some of the most valuable things are embarrassingly simple once someone finally does them.

And finally I think you learn by being wrong. You pick something, you spend a year on it, and you find out nobody cares. That hurts, but it calibrates you. Every researcher I know who has good taste has a graveyard of projects behind them. So my practical advice to students is: work with people whose taste you admire, build things you personally need, and ship early so reality can correct you quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says failed projects and discovering that “nobody cares” can calibrate researchers, but does not identify disappointing reception of their own papers as the learning experience.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s something you develop through experience, rather than something you can learn from a checklist. Early on, you often work on problems that your advisor thinks are important. You may not fully understand why, but you gradually learn by seeing what those problems connect to and what solving them makes possible.

For me, a useful question is: if we solve this problem, what changes? Does it let people do something they couldn’t do before? Does it remove a limitation that keeps coming up? Sometimes a problem is technically challenging, but the answer doesn’t really change very much.

And you need feedback from outside your own work. Talk to people, build things, see where they get stuck. Over time, you start to distinguish between a problem that’s interesting because you know how to approach it and a problem that’s important enough that you should learn how to approach it.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through experience, advisor guidance, assessing impact, and outside feedback, but does not identify reflecting on disappointing reception of one’s own papers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from experience and talking to people. When you start doing research, you tend to focus on whether you can solve a problem. Over time, you learn to ask, “If I solve this, who will care? What will it enable them to do?” Those questions help you judge importance.

It also helps to build something and see where people struggle with it. You might have a very elegant idea, but the thing that actually limits people is somewhere else. That feedback develops your taste. I don’t think there’s a formula—you make judgments, try things, and gradually learn which assumptions were right.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through experience, conversations, building things, and feedback, but does not mention reflecting on disappointing reception of one’s own papers.
